lines.text: I thank Thee that I am not like other men"? Let each of us
examine himself to see if there is not in him also something
of the Pharisaic pattern of life, in some form or other, in some
degree or other! Are we truly in our words and deeds filled
with the spirit of disinterested honesty and objectivity, of
faithful devotion to our work and service? Or are our minds
tainted too in some measure with this will to recognition?
With the intention of standing forth as distinguished by what
we have done? Do we not often eye others with the intention
of comparing ourselves with them and fancying ourselves
to be better and greater? Or do we eye them sometimes with
tenseness and anxiety lest they should get in front of us?
Is not our attitude towards others often envious and love-
less? And are we not as a result oftentimes contentious and
dogmatic? Do we not often deceive ourselves and fancy that
we are better and greater than we are in fact? Do we never
falsify the essence of the good that we like to do when we do
it not from genuinely good motives but in order to fortify our
self-conceit?
There is an infallible test of our dispositions in this matter.
For the man who is truly free from the urge to self-assertion,
from arrogance and ruthlessness, from envy and self-decep-
tion, feels himself free and secure in mixing with others; he
does not get vexed when he has to stand back behind those
who are better than himself, and it is with pleasure that he
recognizes their superiority. It is of no consequence to him
either when he stands behind others who only fancy them-
selves to be better than he and whose false pretentiousness he
penetrates. They cannot affect him harmfully; he does not
allow himself to be embittered, but is always cheerful and
free from self-interested thoughts. Do we always feel our-
selves to be so detached and inwardly secure, and if not
how shall we gain such inner security?
